title: Headache Differential: Primary Disorder or Secondary Emergency?
bottomLine: Headache evaluation starts with onset-to-peak timing, pattern change and secondary red flags. Typical recurrent primary headache with a normal neurologic examination usually does not need routine imaging; thunderclap onset, focal deficit, papilledema, pregnancy/postpartum concern, fever, cancer/immunocompromise or a major new pattern does.
recognize: Migraine, tension-type and cluster headache are common primary disorders with distinct patterns.
Secondary causes include subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, cerebral venous thrombosis, giant-cell arteritis, glaucoma, mass lesion, hypertensive emergency and medication overuse.
differentiate: Thunderclap headache reaches maximal intensity rapidly and requires emergency vascular/hemorrhage evaluation.
Medication-overuse headache is suggested by increasing headache frequency in the setting of frequent acute medication use.
assessment: Ask onset-to-peak, first/worst status, prior pattern, neurologic/visual symptoms, fever, trauma, pregnancy/postpartum status, cancer/immunosuppression and acute medication days per month.
Perform focused neurologic examination and funduscopic assessment when indicated.
workup: Choose CT/CTA, MRI/MRA/MRV, lumbar puncture or inflammatory testing according to the specific secondary differential and timing.
Avoid routine neuroimaging for stable typical migraine with a normal neurologic examination.
management: Treat the identified primary phenotype with evidence-based acute/preventive therapy and address medication overuse.
Escalate secondary red flags to emergency or specialty pathways before symptomatic treatment creates false reassurance.
medicationSafety: Avoid frequent opioids/combination analgesics because they increase medication-overuse and dependence risk.
Pregnancy/postpartum status changes medication and vascular differential decisions.
redFlags: New headache after age 50 with GCA features
counselling: Use a headache diary and teach which changes require emergency assessment.
followUp: Track headache days, disability and acute-medication burden; reassess any major pattern change.
examTrap: Imaging every familiar migraine while failing to recognize a new thunderclap headache as an emergency.
oneLinePearl: Before naming the headache, ask how fast it peaked and what changed.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Neurology headache-imaging recommendations

title: Migraine: Match Acute Therapy and Prevention to Disability and Risk
bottomLine: Migraine is a clinical diagnosis after secondary red flags are excluded. Treat attacks early with an appropriate acute strategy and add prevention when frequency, disability, prolonged attacks or medication-overuse risk justify it; choice depends on comorbidity, pregnancy potential, prior response, access and patient preference.
recognize: Migraine commonly causes recurrent moderate-severe headache with nausea and/or photophobia/phonophobia and worsens with activity; aura is usually fully reversible and develops over minutes.
High acute-medication burden can perpetuate chronic headache.
differentiate: Aura usually evolves over minutes and is reversible; abrupt fixed focal deficit requires stroke evaluation.
Cluster headache is shorter, strictly unilateral with autonomic features and restlessness.
assessment: Assess monthly headache/migraine days, disability, aura, acute medication use, vascular disease, pregnancy, sleep, mood and prior preventive trials.
workup: No routine imaging is needed for a stable classic migraine with normal examination; investigate atypical/red-flag features.
management: Use evidence-based acute therapy such as appropriate analgesic, triptan or other migraine-specific agent according to severity/contraindications.
Use the 2024 Canadian Headache Society prevention framework for oral, injectable/CGRP-targeting and onabotulinumtoxinA options when indicated.
Address sleep, regular meals, activity and medication overuse without blaming lifestyle for migraine.
medicationSafety: Avoid vasoconstrictive agents in relevant vascular contraindications and select pregnancy-compatible options when needed.
Preventive therapy requires agent-specific BP, weight, mood, pregnancy and interaction review.
counselling: Set realistic prevention goals around fewer disabling headache days rather than complete cure and teach acute-medication limits conceptually.
followUp: Reassess preventive response after an adequate trial and track monthly headache days/function.
examTrap: Escalating rescue medication repeatedly without addressing medication overuse or prevention need.
oneLinePearl: Acute migraine therapy stops today's attack; prevention reduces tomorrow's burden.
sourceBasis: Canadian Headache Society Updated Migraine Prevention Guideline 2024

title: Tension-Type Headache: Confirm the Benign Pattern Before Reassurance
bottomLine: Tension-type headache is typically bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild-to-moderate and not worsened by routine activity. Diagnose it only after the history/examination fit and secondary red flags are absent, then prioritize simple acute therapy and prevention of medication overuse.
recognize: Typical attacks are bilateral pressure/tightness without prominent nausea and with limited sensory sensitivity.
Pericranial muscle tenderness can occur but is not required.
differentiate: Migraine more often causes moderate-severe activity-aggravated pain with nausea or combined photophobia/phonophobia.
New focal deficit, fever, thunderclap onset, papilledema or major pattern change is not tension-type headache.
assessment: Assess onset/pattern, headache days, acute medication use, sleep, stress, mood, neck symptoms and neurologic red flags.
workup: No routine neuroimaging for a stable typical pattern and normal neurologic examination; investigate only when secondary features exist.
management: Use simple analgesia judiciously for acute attacks and address sleep, activity, ergonomics/stress and comorbid mood issues.
Frequent/chronic tension-type headache may benefit from preventive therapy and headache-specialty review when refractory.
medicationSafety: Frequent analgesic use can drive medication-overuse headache; chronic opioid therapy is inappropriate for routine tension-type headache.
counselling: Explain the expected benign pattern while giving clear return precautions for a change in character or neurologic/systemic symptoms.
followUp: Track frequency and analgesic days; revisit diagnosis if the phenotype evolves.
examTrap: Calling a first severe thunderclap bilateral headache 'tension' because it feels like pressure.
oneLinePearl: Tension-type headache is a stable benign pattern, not a label for every non-migraine headache.

title: Cluster Headache: Treat the Attack Fast and Start Prevention Early
bottomLine: Cluster headache causes excruciating strictly unilateral orbital/temporal pain with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features or restlessness. Acute treatment must act rapidly, while preventive therapy and secondary-cause assessment are addressed in parallel.
recognize: Attacks are relatively short and recur during cluster periods, often with tearing/red eye, nasal symptoms, ptosis/miosis or facial sweating.
Patients are often restless or pacing rather than seeking stillness.
differentiate: Migraine attacks are usually longer and often worsened by activity; trigeminal neuralgia is seconds-long electric shock pain.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma, carotid dissection and orbital/sinus disease can mimic unilateral autonomic headache.
assessment: Assess exact duration/frequency, autonomic features, restlessness, neurologic/ocular findings and whether this is a first/new atypical pattern.
workup: Typical recurrent cases are clinical diagnoses; first/atypical trigeminal-autonomic presentations often warrant imaging/specialist evaluation.
management: Use rapid evidence-based abortive therapy such as high-flow oxygen and an appropriate rapid-onset triptan when safe.
Start preventive/transitional therapy with neurology/headache guidance for active bouts and frequent disease.
medicationSafety: Repeated vasoconstrictive therapy requires cardiovascular contraindication review.
Do not use routine oral analgesics/opioids as primary cluster-abortive therapy because attacks peak too quickly and harms outweigh benefit.
counselling: Teach oxygen/triptan use and avoid alcohol during active bouts when it reliably triggers attacks.
followUp: Neurology follow-up should confirm diagnosis and preventive strategy, especially for chronic/refractory cluster headache.
examTrap: Treating cluster headache with slow oral analgesia while missing the need for rapid oxygen/triptan therapy.
oneLinePearl: Cluster headache is short, autonomic and severe—treatment must be fast.

title: Seizures: Classify the Event Before Choosing Long-Term Therapy
bottomLine: A first seizure requires separation of provoked from unprovoked and focal from generalized patterns. Long-term antiseizure therapy is chosen by seizure type, recurrence risk, comorbidity, interactions and reproductive considerations—not prescribed automatically after every transient convulsive event.
recognize: Lateral tongue injury, postictal confusion and stereotyped tonic-clonic/focal features support seizure but no single feature is definitive.
Provoking causes include hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance, withdrawal, infection, toxin, stroke and acute brain injury.
differentiate: Syncope can cause brief convulsive movements with rapid recovery; psychogenic nonepileptic events require expert diagnosis without stigmatizing dismissal.
Focal-onset features influence drug selection and structural workup.
assessment: Assess ABCs/glucose/injury, exact witness history, prior subtle events, substances/withdrawal, sleep, medications, pregnancy potential and driving/safety risk.
workup: Use cause-directed labs; EEG and brain MRI are appropriate for unprovoked seizure through the first-seizure pathway.
Urgent imaging is indicated with focal deficit, trauma, anticoagulation, infection/cancer/immunocompromise or persistent altered state.
management: Treat ongoing convulsive seizure/status using emergency protocol and correct reversible causes.
Choose chronic antiseizure therapy according to recurrence risk, seizure type and patient factors; specialist input is appropriate after a first unprovoked or diagnostically uncertain event.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy potential, contraception interactions, mood/cognitive effects, renal/hepatic clearance and teratogenic risk materially affect agent choice.
Avoid abrupt withdrawal of established therapy unless a life-threatening reaction requires an emergency specialist plan.
counselling: Provide bathing/swimming/heights/machinery safety and provincial driving guidance; discuss pregnancy planning early.
followUp: Close the loop on EEG/MRI and monitor seizure control, adverse effects, adherence and reproductive plans.
examTrap: Starting indefinite antiseizure therapy for a single clearly provoked seizure without addressing the cause and recurrence risk.
oneLinePearl: Classify the seizure and its provocation before choosing the drug.

title: Stroke: Last-Known-Well, Reperfusion Eligibility, Then Mechanism-Specific Prevention
bottomLine: A new focal neurologic deficit is stroke until proven otherwise. Establish last-known-well, check glucose, activate a stroke-capable pathway and obtain urgent brain/vascular imaging; after acute treatment, secondary prevention must be mechanism-specific rather than one generic aspirin-and-statin plan.
recognize: Sudden unilateral weakness/numbness, aphasia, visual-field loss, neglect, ataxia or posterior-circulation symptoms can indicate stroke.
A normal glucose and rapidly improving symptoms do not remove reperfusion/vascular-risk questions automatically.
differentiate: Hypoglycemia, seizure/postictal deficit, migraine aura and functional symptoms can mimic stroke but should not delay emergency stroke evaluation when presentation is plausible.
Intracranial hemorrhage must be excluded before routine antithrombotic treatment.
assessment: Document exact onset/last-known-well, anticoagulants/last dose, recent surgery/bleeding, baseline function and neurologic deficits while maintaining ABCs.
workup: Urgent noncontrast brain imaging plus vascular imaging is central; obtain glucose and acute-care labs without delaying reperfusion decisions.
Use cardiac rhythm/vascular evaluation after the emergency phase to determine mechanism.
management: Activate EMS/stroke pathway; thrombolysis and thrombectomy candidacy are time/imaging/clinical decisions made with the acute stroke team, including the 2025 EVT update.
After stroke/TIA, use mechanism-specific antithrombotic, BP, lipid, AF/carotid and lifestyle strategies plus rehabilitation.
medicationSafety: Do not give antiplatelet therapy before hemorrhage is excluded in a new acute presentation.
Anticoagulant exposure affects reperfusion eligibility; report exact drug/dose/last dose.
counselling: Teach FAST and that recurrent transient focal symptoms still require emergency assessment.
followUp: Close the loop on rehabilitation, rhythm monitoring, vascular imaging and secondary-prevention targets.
examTrap: Waiting for a full office neurologic workup before activating acute stroke care.
oneLinePearl: Stroke care is time-to-imaging/reperfusion first, mechanism prevention second.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices Acute Stroke Management 7th Edition with 2025 EVT Interim Update
Canadian Stroke Best Practices secondary prevention resources

title: TIA: Transient Symptoms Do Not Mean Transient Risk
bottomLine: TIA is a clinical warning syndrome requiring urgent brain/vascular and cardiac assessment. Canadian Stroke Best Practices treats recent motor/speech TIA or non-disabling stroke within 48 hours as high recurrence risk and recommends immediate stroke-capable emergency assessment rather than routine outpatient neurology booking.
recognize: Transient unilateral weakness/numbness, aphasia or monocular visual loss are classic focal symptoms; symptoms may resolve before assessment.
Posterior-circulation transient deficits can be less obvious and require careful localization.
differentiate: Migraine aura, seizure and hypoglycemia can mimic TIA, but recurrent stereotyped positive sensory symptoms differ from abrupt negative vascular deficits.
ABCD2 alone should not be used to safely discharge a high-risk clinical presentation.
assessment: Document exact symptom type/duration/onset, vascular risk, AF history, antithrombotics, bleeding history and carotid/cardiac symptoms.
workup: Use urgent brain and vascular imaging according to the stroke pathway plus ECG/rhythm evaluation and selected laboratory testing.
Mechanism-specific workup may include carotid imaging, prolonged rhythm monitoring and echocardiography.
management: Urgently assess high-risk recent symptoms; start antithrombotic/vascular-risk management once hemorrhage and contraindications are addressed according to the stroke pathway.
Carotid stenosis and AF require rapid mechanism-specific referral/treatment.
medicationSafety: Do not empirically combine antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy without a defined indication.
Antithrombotic choice changes when AF or another cardioembolic mechanism is identified.
counselling: Explain that symptom resolution is not reassurance and teach immediate response to recurrence.
followUp: Ensure all imaging/rhythm/cardiology/carotid results are closed-loop and prevention therapy is reviewed promptly.
examTrap: Scheduling routine follow-up because the weakness resolved completely after 20 minutes.
oneLinePearl: TIA symptoms stop; the short-term stroke risk does not.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices TIA and Non-Disabling Stroke recommendations

title: Parkinson Disease: Bradykinesia Plus the Pattern, Then Motor and Non-Motor Care
bottomLine: Parkinson disease is a clinical syndrome centred on bradykinesia plus characteristic motor features and course. Treat the symptoms that impair function, screen non-motor disease and falls, preserve medication timing, and refer atypical or advanced disease rather than diagnosing from tremor alone.
recognize: Rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and asymmetric onset are common; constipation, anosmia, REM-sleep behaviour, depression and autonomic symptoms can precede motor diagnosis.
A good levodopa response supports typical PD but is not a standalone diagnostic test.
differentiate: Essential tremor is primarily action/postural; antipsychotics/metoclopramide can cause drug-induced parkinsonism.
Early falls, gaze palsy, severe early autonomic failure or poor levodopa response raises atypical parkinsonism.
assessment: Assess gait/freezing/falls, cognition, mood, hallucinations, orthostasis, sleep, swallowing, constipation and medication timing/side effects.
workup: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging is used to exclude atypical structural disease rather than to confirm classic PD routinely.
management: Use levodopa and other dopaminergic therapy according to symptom/function needs and integrate exercise, PT/OT/SLP and falls prevention.
Refer advanced fluctuations, dyskinesia, refractory tremor or atypical features to movement-disorders neurology.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop dopaminergic therapy; severe rigidity/hyperthermia syndromes can result.
Avoid dopamine-blocking antiemetics/antipsychotics when safer alternatives are available; screen dopamine agonist users for impulse-control disorders/sleep attacks.
redFlags: Acute inability to take dopaminergic medication
counselling: Teach exercise, fall prevention and exact medication timing; discuss driving and swallowing/cognition as disease evolves.
followUp: Track motor fluctuations, dyskinesia and non-motor burden and coordinate multidisciplinary care.
examTrap: Diagnosing Parkinson disease from tremor alone or giving metoclopramide without considering dopamine blockade.
oneLinePearl: Parkinson disease is bradykinesia plus the right pattern—not every tremor.
sourceBasis: Canadian Guideline for Parkinson Disease, 2nd Edition

title: Essential Tremor: Action Tremor, Functional Burden, and Treatment Tradeoffs
bottomLine: Essential tremor is a bilateral action/postural tremor syndrome diagnosed clinically after medication, thyroid, Parkinsonian and cerebellar mimics are considered. Treat only when tremor causes meaningful disability or distress, balancing medication adverse effects against functional benefit.
recognize: Hand/arm action tremor is typical; head/voice tremor can occur.
Tremor severity can worsen with anxiety/caffeine/fatigue without making anxiety the underlying diagnosis.
differentiate: Parkinson tremor is often rest-predominant with bradykinesia/rigidity; cerebellar tremor has dysmetria/ataxia; medication/thyroid causes need review.
assessment: Assess onset/progression, family history, alcohol/caffeine, medication exposure, thyroid symptoms and the specific tasks impaired (writing, eating, work).
workup: Use targeted thyroid/metabolic testing only when clinical features suggest a secondary cause; routine neuroimaging is not required for a classic stable tremor without neurologic red flags.
management: For disabling tremor, evidence-based options include propranolol or primidone when appropriate; botulinum toxin or procedural therapy may be considered for refractory selected patients through neurology.
Use adaptive devices/OT strategies when helpful.
medicationSafety: Propranolol may worsen bradycardia, hypotension or asthma; primidone can cause sedation/ataxia and should be titrated cautiously, especially in older adults.
counselling: Frame treatment around function and preference rather than cosmetic appearance alone.
followUp: Track functional goals and adverse effects; revisit diagnosis if other neurologic signs emerge.
examTrap: Calling every hand tremor Parkinson disease or treating mild tremor aggressively despite medication risk and minimal functional impact.
oneLinePearl: Essential tremor is an action tremor treated for function, not for the label.

title: Multiple Sclerosis: Establish Dissemination, Separate Relapse From Pseudo-Relapse, Refer for DMT
bottomLine: MS diagnosis requires a compatible CNS demyelinating syndrome with evidence supporting dissemination and exclusion of important mimics. A new inflammatory relapse must be separated from infection/heat-driven pseudo-relapse, and disease-modifying therapy is specialist-managed with infection, vaccination and pregnancy planning built in.
recognize: Optic neuritis, myelitis, diplopia, sensory symptoms, weakness and ataxia are common syndromes in younger adults.
Old deficits can transiently worsen with fever, infection or heat without new inflammatory activity.
differentiate: Stroke, B12 deficiency, structural cord disease, NMOSD/MOGAD and other inflammatory disorders can mimic MS.
Pseudo-relapse reproduces prior deficits during systemic stress; true relapse is a new/substantially worsened neurologic syndrome after alternatives are addressed.
assessment: Define exact new vs old deficits, duration, infection symptoms, bladder function, pregnancy status and current DMT/adherence.
workup: MRI brain/spine and CSF support diagnosis under current neurology criteria; evaluate infection before high-dose steroids when plausible.
DMT-specific baseline infectious, blood, liver and pregnancy testing follows the selected therapy.
management: Treat disabling relapse with specialist-guided corticosteroids when appropriate; do not treat every transient worsening with steroids.
Refer newly diagnosed disease promptly for DMT selection and integrate rehabilitation/symptom management.
medicationSafety: DMTs have agent-specific infection, vaccination, malignancy, laboratory and pregnancy considerations; avoid live-vaccine/immunosuppression errors by using current specialty protocols.
counselling: Discuss fatigue, exercise, heat sensitivity, contraception/pregnancy and vaccines according to the DMT plan.
followUp: Coordinate neurology MRI/clinical monitoring and reassess new symptoms for relapse versus mimic.
examTrap: Giving high-dose steroids for every old symptom that worsens during a UTI without evaluating pseudo-relapse.
oneLinePearl: In MS, first ask whether this is new inflammation or old deficits under stress.
